newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sets low cost estimate for NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sets low cost estimate for NATO expansion.

text.p: The Clinton administration on Monday calculated the cost of expanding NATO to bring in East European countries at up to $35 billion by 2009, a figure below previous private and congressional estimates.

In an effort to show that the United States would get off relatively cheaply, the administration said in a report to Congress that Washington was expected to shoulder costs of only $1.5 billion to $2 billion over the same period.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation is due to announce at a July summit in Madrid the names of countries that will be invited to negotiate membership. The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are leading contenders.

U.S. officials refused to say how many new members their cost estimates budgeted for. The report said only that "a small group of nonspecified Central European countries would join NATO in the first tranche of enlargement".

The Western alliance currently consists of the United States, Canada and 14 European states. The proposed enlargement, which Washington wants to see take place by 1999, would be the first since Spain joined in 1982.

Monday's report, which was requested by Congress last year and compiled by the State and Defence Departments, aimed at answering critics who say that NATO expansion will be a hugely expensive exercise for dubious political gain.

Russia sharply opposes the incorporation of its former Warsaw Pact allies into NATO, saying it will lead to a new division of Europe. Western countries deny this, saying it will help create a peaceful and democratic Europe.

The administration's cost of between $27 billion and $35 billion was lower than an estimate of $42 billion by the private Rand Corporation and way below the figure of $100-120 billion suggested by the Congressional Budget Office.

Assistant Secretary of Defence Edward Warner told a news conference that the CBO had "projected a very, very different environment. They projected an environment of clear-cut, strong hostility directed toward NATO."
Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum said the administration's 32-page report assumed "an environment which is absent a strong and overt threat".
The report broke down enlargement costs into three sections:
-- $10-13 billion in costs the new members would bear themselves to improve their armed forces;
-- $8-10 billion for regional reinforcement capabilities to enable NATO to carry out new missions in Central and Eastern Europe; and
-- $9-12 billion in "direct enlargement costs", mainly measures to enable current and new members to operate jointly.
The report argued that the United States already had the capacity for regional reinforcement and that new members would pick up 40 percent of the direct enlargement costs.
Consequently, it said, U.S. costs would amount to only one-tenth of 1 percent of U.S. defence spending. U.S. officials said this would represent a saving in the long run.

"We are certain that if we did not go forward with this that the cost of not enlarging would be significantly greater than any costs that are involved in enlarging," Assistant Secretary of Defence Frank Kramer told reporters.
"The monetary costs are far less than the concerns that instability and insecurity might bring."
